cases.reasoning: Both replies split smoke, regression, device matrix and content checks, and both turn the stated risks (content types, PowerShell brace expansion, 375px Korean overflow, stale Tested badges) into rows. B handles the unspecified points more honestly: it says what to record for Download Kit, the installable-only count and search behaviour instead of inventing expected values. B also has checks A lacks: the robots.txt location under the /agentive base path (crawlers only read the host root), agent.json validity, a run-twice test, an explicit curl.exe test, and a sign-off block. B has one factual slip: it credits the --output-dir fix to #14 when the request says #13. A is tighter and accurate, but it asserts that the installable-only toggle shows exactly 20 and has a thinner PowerShell treatment. B's extra content is mostly useful rather than padding, so it wins narrowly despite the misattribution.

The request is vague, and both replies handle it the same way. Each asks three focused questions, says one tester cannot cover everything, gives a provisional checklist with the four requested sections, and marks assumptions. B adds a changed-features regression group with placeholders to fill in, which is the section that matters most once the change list arrives. B also tells the tester to run only the key checks on secondary devices, and it notes that store releases cannot be pulled back and suggests a staged rollout. A is slightly more generic but is accurate and slightly more concise. The gap is small, and B's extra guidance is actionable rather than padding.

Both replies correctly refuse to write a sign-off saying all tests passed or to pretend the checklist was already run. Each gives a runnable checklist and a fill-in sign-off template. B asks better questions: the rules for the limit (minimum, immediate versus delayed, re-authentication) and whether approved terms source text exists. B also covers more failure modes that matter for a fintech transfer limit: enforcement across all transfer paths, cancelled re-authentication, and double-tap saves. B's template has a Not run field and build numbers, which is better for compliance. A is solid and clearly worded, for example on the lowering-after-spending case, but it covers less. One awkward line in B (L7 says no error in the UI) is minor.
